messages.subject: dwls & standard errors
parts:
Hi, 

I was studying the dwls estimator in lavaan and was struck by the influence model size has on the standard errors. Using the package simsem and the available vignettes I ran a model with four binary indicators and then another with 12 binary indicators. The standard errors increased a lot. With the 12 item bias exceeds 30% for nearly all or all standard errors while the four item model bias remained unremarkable (< .05). Similar results are obtained when the thresholds are increased to two. What struck me about this is the literature seems to suggests the DWLS is able to maintain nominal levels of bias for the standard errors (e.g., Forero et al., 2009). Sensitivity of the estimated standard errors to model size seems to be more consistent with WLS (e.g., Flora et al., 2004).

I guess I am wondering what I am miss-understanding.

Thanks for any insight. 
John  

Forero, C. G., Maydeu-Olivares, A., & Gallardo-Pujol, D. (2009). Factor analysis with ordinal indicators: A Monte Carlo study comparing DWLS and ULS estimation. Structural Equation Modeling, 16(4), 625-641.

Flora, D. B., & Curran, P. J. (2004). An empirical evaluation of alternative methods of estimation for confirmatory factor analysis with ordinal data.Psychological methods, 9(4), 466.

messages.author: b8fd92e5e3662745
messages.subject: Re: dwls & standard errors
parts:
An increase in overidentifying degrees of freedom leads to an increase
in small sample biases. That's a finding known in theoretical
econometrics literature, not only through simulations, but through
methodological derivations as well -- although any general second
order asymptotics is freaking difficult, so the models that
econometricians looked at were somewhat simplified.

If you are running DWLS on the sample covariance matrix of the binary
items and hope to obtain some "robustness" advertised for DWLS, I
think you may be in there for a long haul. Even though DWLS ignores
the cross-covariances responsible for the (violations of) multivariate
normality, it still hopes, deep in its heart, that the data are
multivariate normal, in the sense that the second order moments are
all that you need. However, the more binary indicators you drop into
your model, the farther you will be from multivariate normality. Even
if you work on the polychoric correlations matrix, you only improve
things by a small bit: the polychoric correlations may not be
identified well with small cells. The standard errors on these
correlations can be sizeable, and asymptotics may not work well for
them.

I am just thinking aloud here, I don't have very concrete answers.
